description: A network of linked circular diagrams over a green background.

Relation of Biology with other sciences. BIOLOGY in the centre, surrounded by Chemistry, Biochemistry, Physics, Biophysics, Geography, Biogeography, Statistics, Biostatistics, Biotechnology, Many sciences, Mathematics, Computer, Computational Biology, Economics and Bio-economics.
The Human Genome Project emblem showing a DNA double helix, with the labels CHEMISTRY, BIOLOGY, PHYSICS, INFORMATICS, ENGINEERING and GENETICS.
A human facing robotic heads and robotic equipment; caption: Robotic and artificial intelligence
small illustration of laboratory glassware, including flasks, test tubes and beakers

Flowchart showing Biological Problem → Observations → Hypotheses → Deductions → Experiments (Experimental group, Control group) → Results → Reporting → Theory / Solution → Law / Principle; arrows are labelled “If proved,” “If not proved” and “Further testing”.
Ronald Ross with his experimental set-up
A mosquito on human skin.

Two diagrams show malaria transmission between sparrows by a Culex mosquito and between men by an Anopheles mosquito. Labels: Sparrow got malaria; Healthy sparrow; Culex; Sparrow ill with malaria; Man got malaria; Healthy man; Anopheles; Man ill with malaria.
Two glass spheres on moss-covered ground with a mushroom, a ladybug and small organisms; a tiny person appears in the left sphere.
International Biodiversity Day poster showing the Earth surrounded by leaves, flowers, butterflies and other small illustrations, with the labels “22, May” and “International Biodiversity Day”.
A descending stack of funnel-shaped levels connected by lines to labels, from top to bottom: Organisms, Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.

Different Classification Systems. (a) 2-Kingdom System: Kingdom Plantae, Kingdom Animalia. (b) 3-Kingdom System: Kingdom Protista, an unlabelled blue section, Kingdom Plantae, Kingdom Animalia. (c) 5-Kingdom System: Kingdom Monera, Kingdom Protista, Kingdom Plantae, Kingdom Fungi, Kingdom Animalia. (d) 3-Domain System: Archaea—Kingdom Archaebacteria; Bacteria—Kingdom Eubacteria; Eukarya—Kingdom Protista, Kingdom Plantae, Kingdom Fungi, Kingdom Animalia.
Three images showing a red oval organism with many long filaments, a cluster of rod-shaped organisms, and white irregular curving and branching forms.

Three Domains. Bacteria — Bacterial cells are smaller than Eukarya cells and have no nucleus. Archaea — Archaea cells have a distinctive chemistry and can survive extreme environments. Eukarya — Eukarya cells are larger and contain more complex structures.
Common protists shown as Euglena, Paramecium, Slime mold, and Water mold.
Common fungi; labels: Smut fungi on leaf, Toadstool, Bracket fungi, Sweet Tooth Fungi
Common plants; labels: Moss, Fern, Conifer, Flowering plant
Two common viruses, a bacteriophage on the left and an influenza virus on the right.
A cutaway illustration of a plant cell showing a green interior, organelles and a blue-green outer wall.
Layers of plant cell wall; labels: Cell, Middle lamella, Secondary wall, Primary wall

Structure of a plant cell; labels: Cell wall, Cell membrane, Vacuole, Mitochondrion, Ribosomes, Golgi apparatus, Chromatin, Nucleolus, Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, Chloroplasts, Pore in cell wall (Plasmodesmata), Golgi vesicle, Nuclear envelope, Rough endoplasmic reticulum, Cytoplasm.

Structure of an animal cell; labels: Intermediate filament, Ribosomes, Rough endoplasmic reticulum, Nucleus, Nucleolus, Chromatin, Golgi apparatus, Mitochondria, Cell membrane, Cytoplasm, Microtubule, Centrosome, Microfilament, Lysosome, Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, Vacuole.
Cellulose fibres in primary wall; micrograph showing cellulose fibres crisscrossing one another.

The fluid mosaic model of cell membrane. Labels: Outside of cell; Glycolipid; Glycoprotein; Protein; Lipid bilayer; Inside of cell; Proteins; Cholesterol. Callout: Another lipid, cholesterol, is attached with the inner sides of the lipid bilayer. Cholesterol is absent in the membranes of most bacteria.
Structure of Nucleus and chromosome; a nucleus and a chromosome, with labels Nuclear envelope, Nuclear pore, Chromatin condenses, Chromosome, Nucleolus, Chromatin, and Nucleoplasm.
Cytoskeleton; labels: Cell membrane, Endoplasmic reticulum, Microfilaments, Intermediate filaments, Microtubule, Mitochondrion
Ribosome; labels: Large subunit, Small subunit
Diagram of smooth and rough endoplasmic reticulum around a nucleus; labels: Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER), Nuclear envelope, Nucleus, Ribosomes, Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER).
Diagram of Golgi apparatus with vesicles; labels: Vesicle from RER, Cisternae, Product for secretion, Product for internal use.

Formation and function of Lysosome; diagram showing a food particle entering the cell, food vacuoles fusing with lysosomes and digestion, and a lysosome engulfing a damaged organelle. Labels: Food particle, Food vacuole, Digestion, Lysosome, Lysosome engulfing damaged organelle, Golgi apparatus.
A Mitochondrion; diagram of a mitochondrion. Labels: Ribosome, DNA, Inner membrane, Outer membrane, Matrix, Crista.
A chloroplast diagram labelled Outer membrane, Inner membrane, DNA, Ribosome, Thylakoid, Granum, and Stroma.
Vacuole in plant and animal cell; labels: Vacuole
Structure of centriole shown in overhead view and side view; labels: Overhead view, Side view, Triplet Microtubules.
Illustrations of a Paramecium covered with cilia and an Euglena with a flagellum; labels: Cilia, Paramecium, Flagellum, Euglena.
Internal structure of leaf showing mesophyll cells; labels: Upper epidermis, Mesophyll cells, Lower epidermis, Guard cells
Epidermis of leaf and root; shows a leaf epidermis micrograph and a root diagram; labels: Guard cells, Leaf epidermis, Root hair cell, Root hair, Root epidermis

Muscle cells: an arm, heart and digestive system connected to illustrations of skeletal muscle cells, cardiac muscle cells and smooth muscle cells. Labels: Skeletal muscle cells; Cardiac muscle cells; Smooth muscle cells.
Neuron: a neuron with branching dendrites, a cell body and a long axon. Labels: Dendrites; Cell body; Axon.
Red blood cells shown in a blood vessel and as individual cells; label: Cytoplasm filled with haemoglobin. Caption: FIGURE 3.20: Red blood cells
Liver, a lobule (unit of liver), and a section of lobule showing liver cells; labels: Liver, Lobule (unit of liver), Section of lobule, Liver cells. Caption: FIGURE 3.21: Liver cells

Differentiation of stem cell into specialized cells, showing stem cells giving rise to nerve cell, muscle cells, epithelial cell, fat cell, gametes, and blood cells. Labels: Stem cells, Nerve cell, Muscle cells, Epithelial cell, Fat cell, Gametes, Blood cells.

Stem cell of blood cells. A red bone marrow-containing bone leads to stem cells, which branch to white blood cells, platelets and red blood cells. Labels: Red bone marrow; Stem cells; White blood cells; Platelets; Red blood cells.
Animal cell and plant cell diagrams with numbered pointers labelled 1–13.
A colorized micrograph showing two orange rounded structures inside a pale blue-green textured cell.

Eukaryotic Cell cycle; a circular cell-cycle diagram with arrows through G1 Phase (Formation of proteins & organelles; Growth in size), S Phase (Duplication of chromosomes; Growth in size), G2 Phase (More growth; Formation of proteins, necessary for division) and M Phase (Cell division), plus G0 Phase (Temporary or permanent stoppage in division); chromosome illustrations labelled Centromere, 1 Chromatid and 2 Chromatids.

diagram of the phases of mitosis, showing Interphase, Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase and Cytokinesis; labels: Nucleolus, Centrosome, Chromatin, Daughter cells, Spindle, Kinetochore, Chromosome (2 chromatids), Attached spindle, Free spindle.
Cytokinesis in animal and plant cells, shown in stages with arrows. Labels: Cleavage furrow, Ring of microfilaments, Daughter cells, (a), Cell wall, Cell plate, Vesicles, Daughter cells, (b).
FIGURE 4.4: Regeneration in sea star; a sea star with a broken arm and a sea star with the arm regenerated. Labels: Broken arm, Arm regenerated.
FIGURE 4.5: Budding in Hydra; a sequence showing a bud growing on a Hydra and developing into a new Hydra. Labels: Bud, New Hydra.
Crossing over. Diagram shows chromosomes exchanging portions; labels: Non-sister chromatids, Sister chromatids, Centromere, Chiasmata, Exchange of portions.
Phases of meiosis-I, shown as a sequence of cell diagrams with arrows. Labels: Centrosome, Nucleolus, Chromatin, Spindle, Crossing over, Prophase-I, Prophase-I, Metaphase-I, Anaphase-I, Telophase-I.
Two parallel sequences show the stages of meiosis II, with chromosomes and spindle fibres in the cells. Labels: Prophase-II, Metaphase-II, Anaphase-II, Telophase-II, Cytokinesis.

Meiosis creates cells with new combinations of genes. Shows two parent cells with homologous chromosomes undergoing meiosis to produce gametes, which combine to form a zygote with homologous chromosomes. Labels: “Cells of Parents with homologous chromosomes”, “Meiosis”, “Gametes” (twice), “Zygote with homologous chromosomes”.

Comparison between meiosis and mitosis. Diagram showing stages of Meiosis-I, Meiosis-II, and Mitosis. Labels: “Homologous chromosomes” (twice); “Synapsis & Crossing over”; “Pairs of Homologous chromosomes attached to spindle”; “Homologous chromosomes attach individually”; “Meiosis-I”; “Meiosis-II”; “Mitosis”.
A neuron with branching extensions above a cross-section of tissue.
Levels of organization from Atom, Molecule, Organelle, Cell, Tissue, Organ, Organ system, to Individual, with animal examples above and plant examples below.
A leaf and an exploded view of its tissues. Labels: Veins, Midrib, Cuticle, Upper epidermis, Palisade mesophyll, Spongy mesophyll, Xylem, Phloem, Guard cells, Stoma, Lower epidermis.

A plant showing the shoot system above ground and the root system below ground. Labels: Shoot system, Flower — Helps in reproduction, Leaf — Performs photosynthesis, Fruit — Protects the seeds, Stem — Supports the plant, Root — Absorbs water and minerals, Root system.
A layered tissue cross-section alongside a cutaway view of the stomach, labeled “Epithelial tissue,” “Connective tissue,” “Muscle tissue,” and “Connective Tissue.”

Illustrations of the skeletal system labelled Cartilage, Bone, Joint, and Skeletal system; the digestive system labelled Liver, Stomach, Small intestine, Large intestine, and Digestive system; the respiratory system labelled Wind pipe, Lungs, and Respiratory system; the muscular system labelled Skeletal muscles, Tendons, and Muscular system; the nervous system labelled Brain, Spinal cord, Nerves, and Nervous system; and the blood circulatory system labelled Heart, Blood vessels, and Blood circulatory system.

Homeostasis of body temperature. A human silhouette surrounded by a cycle of arrows and boxes showing body-temperature regulation. Labels: “Body temperature falls below 37°C”; “Muscles start shivering. Shivering generates heat.”; “Body temperature rises to 37°C”; “Normal body temperature”; “Body temperature rises above 37°C”; “Sweat glands secrete sweat. As the sweat evaporates, heat is lost from the body.”; “Body temperature falls to 37°C”.
Illustration of a DNA double helix, with paired spherical components connected by strands.
Common pentoses: two ring-structure diagrams labeled Ribose and Deoxyribose. Labels include CH₂OH, O, OH, H, C, and carbon numbers 1–5.
Common hexoses: three ring-structure diagrams labeled Glucose, Galactose, and Fructose. Labels include CH₂OH, O, OH, HO, H, C, and carbon numbers 1–6.

Structural diagrams of Sucrose and Maltose, showing glucose and fructose subunits. Labels: Glucose subunit, Fructose subunit, Glucose subunit, Glucose subunit; CH₂OH, O, H, OH, HO; numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 on glucose units and 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 on the fructose unit. Caption: Common disaccharides.
diagrams of polysaccharides labeled Starch, Glycogen, and Cellulose
General structure of an amino acid with R above the central C, H₂N to the left, COOH to the right, and H below; caption: Amino acid - general structure.

Glycine structure with H above and below the central C, H₂N to the left and COOH to the right, captioned Glycine; alanine structure with CH₃ above and H below the central C, H₂N to the left and COOH to the right, captioned Alanine.
Structural formula captioned “Glycerol”: three vertically connected C atoms, each with H on the left and OH on the right; the top C has H above, and the bottom C has H below.
Structural formula of a saturated fatty acid, showing a carbon chain with single bonds and labels H, C, O and OH; caption: “Saturated fatty acid”.
Structural formula of an unsaturated fatty acid, showing a carbon chain with a double bond and labels H, C, O and OH; caption: “Unsaturated fatty acid”.
General structure of fats and oils: a glycerol backbone labeled “Glycerol”, with three “Fatty acid” groups attached; the diagram also labels H and C. Caption: “Fats and oils General structure”.

General structure of phospholipids: a glycerol backbone labeled “Glycerol”, with two “Fatty acid” groups and one “Phosphate group” attached; the diagram also labels H and C. Caption: “Phospholipids General structure”.
Nucleotide General structure showing a phosphate group labelled P connected to a pentose labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, and an N-base; the pentose is labelled O, and the N-base shows N labels.

Double helix model of DNA; shows Strand 1 and Strand 2, and an enlarged DNA strand model labelled “1 nucleotide” with base pairs A–T, C–G, G–C and T–A, phosphate labels “P”, and an “N-bases” legend: Cytosine, Guanine, Adenine, Thymine.
Structure of RNA: An RNA strand shown as a twisted single strand and an enlarged nucleotide chain. Labels: RNA Strand; 1 nucleotide; P; C; U; G; A; N-bases; Cytosine; Guanine; Adenine; Uracil.

Working of DNA (also called the Central Dogma), showing a chromosome, a segment of DNA (a gene), transcription to mRNA, mRNA moving to cytoplasm, a ribosome, translation, and protein; labels: Chromosome, Segment of DNA (a gene), Transcription, mRNA, mRNA moves to cytoplasm, Ribosome, Translation, Protein
A multicoloured molecular structure of a protein against a blue background.

A green hummingbird with a red throat perched on a branch. The accompanying text reads: Hummingbirds have one of the highest metabolic rates of any animal. They need to eat constantly to keep up their energy levels.

Types of metabolism. Catabolism shows a larger molecule breaking down into smaller units, with energy released; anabolism shows smaller units combining into a larger molecule, using energy. Labels: Larger molecule; Smaller units; Catabolism; Energy; Smaller units; Larger molecule; Anabolism.
Active site of enzyme; a blue enzyme structure with an active site labelled “Active site” and the structure labelled “Enzyme”.

Lock and key model of enzyme action; a sequence shows a green substrate fitting into a red enzyme at the active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex, then releasing green products and leaving the red enzyme; arrows show the sequence. Labels: “Substrate”, “Active site”, “Enzyme”, “Enzyme-Substrate Complex”, “Products”, “Enzyme”.

Induced fit model of enzyme action; a sequence shows a Substrate and an Enzyme with an Active site, Changes in active site, an Enzyme-Substrate Complex, and Products released from the Enzyme. Arrows indicate the sequence.

Effect of temperature on enzyme activity; a graph of Rate of reaction against Temperature (°C), with temperature ticks 20, 30, 40 and 50, and a curve peaking at the dashed line for Optimum temperature for human enzymes (37°C).

Graph of rate of reaction against pH of reaction environment, with the y-axis labelled “Rate of reaction,” x-axis labelled “pH of reaction environment,” x-axis values 1 to 9, a magenta curve peaking near pH 2 labelled “Optimum pH for pepsin (1.5 to 2.0)” and a blue curve peaking near pH 8 labelled “Optimum pH for trypsin (7.8),” dashed vertical lines at the peaks; caption: FIGURE 7.6: Effect of pH on enzyme activity

Graph of rate of reaction against substrate concentration, with the y-axis labelled “Rate of reaction,” x-axis labelled “Substrate concentration,” a rising curve that levels off, and a dashed vertical line at the plateau labelled “All active sites occupied”; caption: FIGURE 7.7: Effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity

Two diagrams compare competitive and non-competitive inhibition. Labels: “Substrate,” “Enzyme,” “Competitive inhibitor attaches with active site. So, substrate cannot attach.”, “Non-competitive inhibitor changes shape of enzyme and its active site. So, substrate cannot attach.” Captions: “Competitive Inhibition” and “Non-competitive Inhibition.”
A colorful illustration of a cell interior, showing a large round pink structure, orange elongated structures and small green particles.
Molecular structure of ATP. Labels: Phosphate groups, P, P, P, Energy bonds, Adenine, Ribose, Adenosine, Adenosine monophosphate (AMP), Adenosine diphosphate (ADP), Adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
ATP-ADP Cycle. Labels: Formation of ATP, ATP, Pᵢ, ADP, Energy, Breakdown of ATP.
Light reactions of photosynthesis; labels include Released, ½ O₂, H₂O, 2H⁺, 2e⁻, Light, Chlorophyll, Energy level, Electron transport chain, Energy for the synthesis of ATP, ATP, NADP, NADPH and H⁺.

Dark reactions of photosynthesis; diagram shows a cycle with 3 CO₂, 3 molecules of 5-C compounds, 3 molecules of 6-C compounds, 6 molecules of 3-C compounds, 6 molecules of 3-C carbohydrates, and 5 molecules of 3-C compounds; ATP and NADPH are labeled on arrows leading to the 3-C carbohydrates, which lead to Glucose.
Summary of Glycolysis. Glucose (6-C) → 2 Pyruvic acid (3-C), with labels 2 ATP, 2 ADP, 4 ADP, 4 ATP, 2 NAD, and 2 NADH.
Diagram of pyruvic acid (3-C) changing to acetyl CoA (2-C), with CoA, NAD, CO₂ and NADH; acetyl CoA enters the Krebs Cycle, which shows CoA, 2 CO₂, 3 NAD, 3 NADH, FAD, FADH₂, ATP and ADP.
Diagram showing NADH changing to NAD, with 3 ADP, 3 ATP, O₂ and H₂O; and FADH₂ changing to FAD, with 2 ADP, 2 ATP, O₂ and H₂O.

An overview of number of ATPs reduced by the aerobic oxidation of glucose. Glucose → Glycolysis → Pyruvic acid → Acetyl CoA → Krebs Cycle. Glycolysis shows 2 ATP and produces 2 ATP, and 2 NADH → 4 ATP in the Electron Transport Chain. Pyruvic acid produces 2 NADH → 6 ATP in the Electron Transport Chain. Krebs Cycle produces 2 ATP, 6 NADH → 18 ATP, and 2 FADH₂ → 4 ATP in the Electron Transport Chain. Total = 36 ATP.
Sunlight shining through green leaves.
Two photographs of leaves showing (a) chlorosis due to nitrogen deficiency and (b) chlorosis due to magnesium deficiency.

Uptake of water and salts by root: a plant with an enlarged root cross-section showing water and salts moving through cells and cell walls; labels: Cortex, Pericycle, Xylem, Phloem, Epidermis, Endodermis, Root hair, Water & salts moving through cells, Water & salts moving through cell walls.
Events of transpiration; a leaf cross-section showing Upper epidermis, Mesophyll cells, Water vapours, Lower epidermis, Stoma, Guard cells, and Xylem.

Opening and closing of stoma. Two diagrams show an open stoma and a closed stoma, labelled Guard cells, Epidermal cells, Chloroplast, Vacuole, Stoma, Nucleus, H₂O, K⁺ ions, Open stoma and Closed stoma.
Diagram of water transport in a plant from the roots, through the stem and leaf, to transpiration. Labels: Transpiration; Xylem of leaf; Xylem of stem; Xylem of root; Root hair; Water molecule.

Transport of food; diagram showing food moving through phloem from the mesophyll cell (source) to the sink, and H₂O moving between xylem and phloem. Labels: H₂O, Sieve tube, Companion cell, Food molecules, Mesophyll Cell (source), Sink, Xylem, Phloem, H₂O.
(a) A plant showing gaseous exchange at Night and Day, with O₂ and CO₂ arrows; (b) a leaf cross-section labelled Cuticle, Air leaves, Air enters, and Stoma.
A bark surface and a cross-section showing a Lenticel; labels: Bark, Lenticel.

A tree with illustrations showing stomatal, cuticular, and lenticular transpiration. Labels: “Stomatal Transpiration,” “Cuticular Transpiration,” “Lenticular Transpiration.” Caption: “FIGURE 9.9: Types of transpiration”
Photographs of different leaves with water droplets at their tips and edges. Caption: Guttation in different leaves
Excretion in Plants — three photos labeled “Latex from Rubber plant”, “Gum from Keeker tree”, and “Resins from coniferous tree”.

(1)- Closed stomata in the leaf of tomato (a mesophyte); (2)- Broad leaves of waterlily (a hydrophyte); (3)- Succulent stem of Cactus (a xerophyte); (4)- Salt crystals on the leaf of a sea plant (a halophyte). FIGURE 9.12: Osmotic adjustments in Plants
A close-up of a round plant structure with many orange circular structures beside an insect on green leaves.
Binary fission in bacteria; stages labelled “1. Parent Bacterium”, “2. DNA replicates”, “3. Cell membrane pinches in” and “4. Daughter Bacteria”.
Binary fission in Amoeba; stages labelled “1. Parent Amoeba”, “2. Nucleus divides”, “3. Cytoplasm divides” and “4. Daughter Amoebae”.
Budding in Yeast; labels: Yeast cell, A bud forms, Bud grows and new buds form
Asexual reproduction by spores (in *Rhizopus*); labels: Sporangium, Spores
Vegetative propagation in strawberry (through runner); labels: Stolon (runner), New plant, Node
Potato; labels: Eyes, Tuber
Ginger rhizome with a growing plant; labels: Growing plant, Rhizome
Onion; labels: Fleshy leaves, Bud, Bulb
Garlic corm; labels: Brown leaves, Corm
Sucker in banana; banana plant labeled “Parent tree” and “Sucker”.
Modified leaf of bryophyllum; leaf labeled “Modified leaf” and “Bud”.

Using Cuttings for vegetative propagation; a parent plant is cut at the point of cut to make a cutting, which is planted to produce a new plant. Labels: Point of cut, Parent plant, Cutting, New plant.
Grafting; a piece from a second plant is joined to a parent plant, producing a new plant. Labels: Piece from second plant, Parent plant, New plant.

Alternation of generations in plants; a cycle showing Sporophyte (2n), Meiosis, Spores (1n), Gametophyte (1n), Mitosis, Female gamete (1n), Male gamete (1n), Zygote (2n), and Mitosis, with arrows connecting the stages.
Parts of a flower; diagram of a flower with a separate carpel and stamen. Labels: Carpel, Ovary, Stigma, Style, Stamen, Anther, Filament, Petal, Sepal, Receptacle, Microspore.

Development of female gametophyte (embryo sac); a flower, pistil and ovule are shown alongside stages in embryo sac development: Megaspore mother cell (2n), Meiosis, Megaspore (1n), Mitosis (3 times), Fusion nucleus, Egg, and Embryo sac (female gametophyte). Labels on the plant and enlarged ovule: Stigma, Style, Ovary, Ovule, Integuments, Micropyle, Megasporangium (Ovule).

A flower and anther, with the microsporangium (pollen sac) and its development sequence: microspore mother cell (2n) → meiosis → microspores (1n) → mitosis → male gametophyte (pollen grain), labelled tube cell and generative cell; the flower is labelled anther and filament.

Life cycle of a flowering plant; labels: Anther, Meiosis, Microspores, Pollen grain (male gametophyte), Pollination, Pollen sac, Sperms, Tube cell, Ovule, Stigma, Style, Ovary, Embryo sac (female gametophyte), Micropyle, Fusion nucleus, Sperms, Egg, Pollen tube, Endosperm, Embryo, Seed, Endosperm nucleus (3n), Zygote (2n).
longitudinal section of a flower with blank pointer lines
Financial data display with colored bars, numerical values and several colored line graphs

Bar chart titled “Chart: Number of Plants”. The vertical axis is “Number of Plants” and is marked 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. The horizontal axis is “Species” and shows Species A (15), Species B (20), Species C (10), Species D (25), and Species E (5).
